This vignette covers the autocorrelation of the residuals of a plant over time, and simulation studies: simulating data from a fitted model, refitting it, and comparing the estimates with the true parameters, including the autocorrelation parameter.

A logistic growth curve with correlated random effects of the plants on the asymptote and the time of the maximum growth rate, as in the vignette *Fixed and random effects*, here without treatment effects:

```{r}
library(gcTMB)
library(ggplot2)
fitre <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = FabaHeights25)
```

## Autocorrelation of the residuals

The random effects shift the whole curve of a plant, but a plant that is above its curve at one measurement often stays above it at the next. The `correlation` argument models this autocorrelation of the residuals within a group over time, with the same correlation structures as the package nlme (Pinheiro and Bates, 2000; Zuur et al., 2009, Chapter 6). The residuals $\varepsilon$ of a group are normal with the residual variance $\sigma^2$ and

$$\mathrm{cor}(\varepsilon_s, \varepsilon_t) = \rho^{|t - s|},$$

with $\rho$ the correlation of residuals one unit of time apart. `corAR1()` is the autoregressive process of order 1 at integer times (or at the positions of the observations, with `form = ~ 1 | group`), with $-1 < \rho < 1$; `corCAR1()` its continuous-time version, for unequally spaced times, with $0 < \rho < 1$. Residuals of different groups are independent, and the correlation is available for the gaussian and lognormal (on the log scale) families. As the process is Markov, each residual given the previous one of its group, $dt$ earlier, is normal with mean $\rho^{dt} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{prev}}$ and variance $\sigma^2 (1 - \rho^{2 dt})$, so the likelihood is exact and its cost linear in the number of observations; with random effects, the Laplace approximation integrates them out as before.

The parameter $\rho$ is estimated on an unconstrained scale, as in nlme. For `corCAR1()`, with $0 < \rho < 1$, this is the logit link, $\log(\rho/(1 - \rho))$. For `corAR1()`, with $-1 < \rho < 1$, it is $\log((1 + \rho)/(1 - \rho))$, the logit of $(1 + \rho)/2$, which maps the interval $(-1, 1)$ to the real line (twice Fisher's $z$-transformation, $2\,\mathrm{atanh}(\rho)$). `coef()` reports the parameter on this scale, as `cor_par:CAR1` or `cor_par:AR1`, and `corpars()`, `summary()` and `confint()` report $\rho$ itself.

The heights are measured every 7 days, so with `corCAR1(form = ~ DAS | plant_ID)` $\rho$ is the correlation per day, and $\rho^7$ that of consecutive measurements:

```{r}
fitrec <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = FabaHeights25,
                correlation = corCAR1(form = ~ DAS | plant_ID))
summary(fitrec)
corpars(fitrec)^7
anova(fitre, fitrec)
```

`confint()` gives the profile likelihood interval of $\rho$, or with `method = "wald"` a Wald interval computed on the logit scale and transformed back:

```{r}
confint(fitrec, parm = "cor_par:CAR1")
```

## Simulation

A simulation study has four steps: fit a model to data, simulate new data sets from the fitted model, refit the model to the simulated data, and compare the estimates with the true parameters, the estimates of the original fit.

### The true model

We fit a logistic growth curve to the heights of the faba beans in `FabaHeights25`, with random effects on the asymptote $b_1$, the time of the maximum growth rate $b_2$ and the scale $b_3$ of each plant. The random effects of a plant are correlated: their covariance matrix is unstructured. The threshold $b_4$ and the asymmetry $b_5$ are fixed at their defaults, $b_4 = 0$ (the curve starts at zero at time 0) and $b_5 = 1$ (the symmetric curve).

```{r sim-fit}
fitsim <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 + b3 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = FabaHeights25)
fitsim
converged(fitsim)
```

The fitted model is the true model of the simulation. Its parameters are:

```{r sim-truth}
fixef(fitsim)
VarCorr(fitsim)
sigma(fitsim)
```

Other true models can be made from it with `update()`, e.g. `update(fitsim, fixef = c(b1 = 150))` for a larger asymptote, `update(fitsim, VarCorr = ...)` for other covariance matrices of the random effects, or `update(fit, rho = ...)` for another autocorrelation, as below.

### Simulating new plants

We simulate 50 new plants, each measured at 10 equidistant days from day 5 to day 100. Each plant in `newdata` is a new curve, with its own random effects drawn from the fitted covariance matrix.

```{r sim-simulate}
simdata <- expand.grid(DAS = seq(5, 100, length.out = 10),
                       plant_ID = paste("plant", 1:50, sep = ""))
simdata$height <- simulate(fitsim, nsim = 1, seed = 1, newdata = simdata)[[1]]
head(simdata)
```

### Refitting the model

The same model is fitted to the simulated data.

```{r sim-refit}
simfit <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 + b3 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = simdata)
converged(simfit)
```

`converged()` checks that the log-likelihood is finite, that the optimiser reports convergence with a largest absolute gradient below $10^{-3}$, and that the Hessian is positive definite. With few individuals and several correlated random effects, the likelihood is often so flat in some directions that `nlminb` reports "singular convergence" or "false convergence", or stops with a gradient slightly above $10^{-3}$, although it is at the maximum. With `control = list(restart = TRUE)`, such a fit is optimised once more from its estimates. The fit keeps the better optimum, and `fit$restart$improvement` holds the improvement of the log-likelihood. `converged()` accepts a fit that the restart improved by less than `lltol` ($10^{-6}$ by default), since its maximum is stable. In a simulation study that does not need standard errors, `sdreport = FALSE` also saves about a quarter of the time of each fit, but then the Hessian is not checked. Here, with three plants:

```{r sim-restart}
small <- expand.grid(DAS = seq(10, 80, length.out = 8), plant_ID = paste0("p", 1:3))
small$height <- simulate(fitsim, newdata = small, seed = 1)[[1]]
f0 <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 + b3 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = small,
            control = list(sdreport = FALSE))
converged(f0)
f1 <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 + b3 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = small,
            control = list(sdreport = FALSE, restart = TRUE))
f1$restart$improvement
converged(f1)
```

The 95% parametric bootstrap confidence intervals of the coefficients and the variance parameters are compared with the true values, the estimates of the original fit. `confint` reports the standard deviations of the random effects and the residual standard deviation on their natural scale, while `coef` has them on the log scale, so the true values and the estimates are transformed in the same way. The correlations of the three random effects stay on the unconstrained scale of `coef`.

```{r sim-confint}
ci <- confint(simfit, method = "boot", nsim = 50, seed = 1)
natural <- function(p){
  lg <- grepl("^log_", names(p))
  p[lg] <- exp(p[lg])
  p
}
truth <- natural(coef(fitsim))
tab <- data.frame(true = truth, estimate = natural(coef(simfit)), ci,
                  covered = truth >= ci[, 1] & truth <= ci[, 2],
                  check.names = FALSE)
# the standard deviations are on their natural scale: drop "log_" from their names
rownames(tab) <- sub("^log_", "", rownames(tab))
tab
```

The simulated heights and the estimated curves of the 50 plants:

```{r sim-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
grid <- expand.grid(DAS = seq(5, 100, length.out = 200), plant_ID = unique(simdata$plant_ID))
grid$height <- predict(simfit, newdata = grid)
ggplot(simdata, aes(DAS, height, group = plant_ID)) +
  geom_line(data = grid, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Days after sowing", y = "Height") +
  theme_bw()
```

In a full simulation study, these steps are repeated for many simulated data sets, e.g. to estimate the coverage of the confidence intervals or to compare growth models with `criteria()`, as below for the autocorrelation.

### Recovering the autocorrelation

With a correlation structure, `simulate()` draws the residuals of each group with the autocorrelation of the fit: within a plant in `newdata`, ordered in time, each residual given the previous one, $dt$ earlier, is normal with mean $\rho^{dt}$ times the previous residual and variance $\sigma^2 (1 - \rho^{2 dt})$. `update()` is designed for simulation studies like this one: it sets some of the parameters of a fitted model to chosen values and keeps the others, without refitting, so that the result can serve as the true model of the simulation. Its arguments are `fixef` for the coefficients, `VarCorr` for the covariance matrices of the random effects, `sigma` for the residual standard deviation, and `rho` for the autocorrelation.

Here the true model is the fit `fitrec` from above, with correlated random effects of the plants on $b_1$ and $b_2$ and continuous-time AR(1) residuals. Its autocorrelation, $\rho = `r round(corpars(fitrec), 2)`$ per day, is set to $\rho = 0.8$ with `update()`, and all other parameters keep their estimates:

```{r sim-cartrue}
rho0 <- 0.8
fitcar <- update(fitrec, rho = rho0)
```

`update()` changes $\rho$ and nothing else, so the other parameters are those estimated together with $\rho = `r round(corpars(fitrec), 2)`$. Alternatively, a new fit with $\rho$ fixed at 0.8, `corCAR1(value = 0.8, fixed = TRUE)`, estimates the other parameters given $\rho = 0.8$. This is the way to go when the true model should fit the data as well as possible with the chosen $\rho$, and it has the higher log-likelihood; `update()` is the way to go when only $\rho$ should differ from the fitted model, e.g. to compare simulations with different autocorrelations and otherwise the same parameters.

```{r sim-carfixed}
fitfix <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = FabaHeights25,
                correlation = corCAR1(value = rho0, form = ~ DAS | plant_ID, fixed = TRUE))
pars <- function(f) c(fixef(f)[c("b1:(Intercept)", "b2:(Intercept)", "b3:(Intercept)")],
                      sigma = sigma(f), corpars(f), logLik = as.numeric(logLik(f)))
rbind(estimated = pars(fitrec), updated = pars(fitcar), refitted = pars(fitfix))
```

We simulate from the updated model: 50 data sets of 30 new plants, each measured at 12 unequally spaced days between day 10 and day 63. We fit the model to each data set, now with $\rho$ estimated. `confint()` computes the Wald interval of $\rho$ on the logit scale and transforms it back.

```{r sim-carrun,warning=FALSE}
days <- c(10, 13, 17, 21, 24, 28, 35, 38, 42, 49, 56, 63)
design <- expand.grid(DAS = days, plant_ID = paste0("p", 1:30))
sims <- simulate(fitcar, nsim = 50, seed = 1, newdata = design)
carsim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sims, function(y){
  dat <- cbind(design, height = y)
  f1 <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = dat,
              correlation = corCAR1(form = ~ DAS | plant_ID))
  ci <- confint(f1, parm = "cor_par:CAR1", method = "wald")
  data.frame(rho = corpars(f1)[["rho"]], lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
             covered = ci[1] <= rho0 & rho0 <= ci[2])
}))
```

The means of the estimates of $\rho$ and of the bounds of their 95% Wald intervals, and the coverage of the intervals, against the true value 0.8:

```{r sim-cartab}
colMeans(carsim[, c("rho", "lower", "upper", "covered")])
```

```{r sim-carplot, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3}
ggplot(carsim, aes(x = rho)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "grey70", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rho0, colour = "red") +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Estimate of ", rho)), y = "Simulations") +
  theme_minimal()
```
